newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BA official says no decision yet on slots.
newsitem.headline: BA official says no decision yet on slots.

text.p: British Airways has not yet decided whether to release slots at London's Heathrow airport to win U.K. regulatory approval for its proposed alliance with AMR Corp's American Airlines, a BA official said on Friday.
BA's head of competition and industry affairs Christopher Allen told Reuters that "there was no point in coming to a final position" until all regulatory authorities had completed their asessement.
But he reiterated his company's view that airlines should be able to sell airport landing and taking off slots despite the European Commission's view that this is illegal.

"We have not said whether we are prepared even to sell them, but we believe we should be able to sell them (if we want to)," Allen said in the margins of a two-day conference on European air transport services and airports.

The U.K.'s Office of Fair Trading said in December it would clear the BA-AA alliance if the companies gave up 168 weekly slots at Heathrow, but European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert warned the trading of slots was not "acceptable".
AMR's senior vice president Hans Mirka was quoted by the Wall Street Journal Europe on Friday as saying he was prepared to defy the Commission and sell slots at Heathrow.
American has 181 weekly slots at Heathrow, according to Allen.

In reply to a question, he said the slot issue appeared to be holding the key for getting antitrust immunity, but he did not think it would be a matter for discussion at talks on an 'open-skies' agreement between Britain and the United States.
"Both governments agree that slots are not a matter for bilateral discussion," he said.

With an open-skies agreement, the congestion at Heathrow would no longer be a problem for other U.S. carriers since they would be given the right to compete with the alliance. But the accord would not give EU-based airlines the traffic rights they may need, which is also why the Commission has expressed competition concerns, the participants at the conference organised by IBC UK Conferences Ltd said.

Earlier at the conference, Allen defended the view that slot trading was both "lawful and highly desirable". Current EU rules, which are being revised by the Commission, had done nothing to increase competition at busy airports, he said.
Although this view was shared by many participants, which included industry reprentatives and antitrust lawyers, many also acknowledged that the selling of slots would not resolve the problem.
Christopher Welsh, secretary general of the European Air Shippers Council, said that slot trading, if made legal, would give "a considerable advantage to incumbent carriers".

This view was shared by Philip Martin, director general of Britain's Air Transport Users Council, who argued that the surrender of slots could not be described as "confiscation" since such rights were not the property of the airlines.

The Commission is expected to make proposals shortly which could allow for the selling of slots. EU transport ministers would have the final word on this, but whatever the new rules may be they will come to late for the BA-AA alliance. -- Brussels newsroom 322 2876841
